ishtar-gate.name: Ishtar Gate
ishtar-gate.summary: The eighth gate of Babylon's inner city wall, built around 569 BC under King Nebuchadnezzar II, decorated with glazed-brick animals and deities; excavated by Robert Koldewey from 1904 to 1914.

nebuchadnezzar-ii.name: Nebuchadnezzar II
nebuchadnezzar-ii.summary: Second king of the Neo-Babylonian Empire, ruling 605 to 562 BC; renowned for military victories including Carchemish and for major construction projects in Babylon.

amytis-of-media.name: Amytis of Media
amytis-of-media.summary: A queen of Babylon (c. 630–565 BCE), wife of Nebuchadnezzar II and daughter of the Median king Cyaxares.

berossus.name: Berossus
berossus.summary: Early 3rd-century BCE Hellenistic-era Babylonian priest, astronomer and writer who wrote in Greek; his major work, the Babyloniaca, is lost but survives in fragments quoted by later writers such as Eusebius.

ziggurat.name: Ziggurat
ziggurat.summary: A massive terraced structure built in ancient Mesopotamia and Iran, believed by the Sumerians to house the gods, with the Great Ziggurat of Ur among the best known examples.

pergamon-museum.name: Pergamon Museum
pergamon-museum.summary: A museum on Berlin's Museum Island, built from 1910 to 1930, holding major antiquities such as the reconstructed Ishtar Gate, closed since 2023 for renovation.

nineveh.name: Nineveh
nineveh.summary: Ancient city on the Tigris near modern Mosul, Iraq, and capital of the Neo-Assyrian Empire; briefly the largest city in the world until it was sacked in 612 BC.

sumer.name: Sumer
sumer.summary: The earliest known civilization, in southern Mesopotamia (now south-central Iraq), emerging between the 5th and 4th millennium BCE; its cities produced the world's earliest known written texts.

mu-u-u.name: Mušḫuššu
mu-u-u.summary: A mythological hybrid creature from ancient Mesopotamian mythology, with a scaly body, eagle-like talons, lion forelimbs, horns and a snake-like tongue; famously shown on Babylon's Ishtar Gate.

marduk.name: Marduk
marduk.summary: The patron god of Babylon, worshipped as a god of creation, justice and magic, who rose to become leader of the Mesopotamian pantheon by the 2nd millennium BC.

hadad.name: Hadad
hadad.summary: Storm- and rain-god of Canaanite and ancient Mesopotamian religion, also called Adad or Baʿal, symbolized by the bull and later equated with Zeus and Jupiter.

inanna.name: Inanna (Ishtar)
inanna.summary: Ancient Mesopotamian goddess of war, love and sex, originally worshipped in Sumer and later known as Ishtar among the Akkadians, Babylonians and Assyrians.

neo-babylonian-empire.name: Neo-Babylonian Empire
neo-babylonian-empire.summary: The last empire ruled by native Mesopotamian kings, from 626 to 539 BC, remembered for Nebuchadnezzar II's destruction of Jerusalem's Temple and a cultural renaissance in Babylon.

sennacherib.name: Sennacherib
sennacherib.summary: King of the Neo-Assyrian Empire from 705 to 681 BC, famed in the Hebrew Bible for his Levant campaign, who destroyed Babylon in 689 BC and expanded the capital Nineveh.

walls-of-babylon.name: Walls of Babylon
walls-of-babylon.summary: The massive fortified walls surrounding ancient Babylon, among the largest structures of their era and included in many ancient lists of the Seven Wonders of the World.

strabo.name: Strabo
strabo.summary: Greek geographer (64/63 BC to about 24 AD) best known for his Geographica, a descriptive survey of the peoples and places known in his time.

archimedes-screw.name: Archimedes' screw
archimedes-screw.summary: A screw-shaped pump for lifting water, traditionally credited to Archimedes though possibly already in Egyptian use, still applied today for irrigation and small hydroelectric power.

onesicritus.name: Onesicritus
onesicritus.summary: Greek Cynic philosopher and historical writer (c. 360–290 BC) who accompanied Alexander the Great's campaigns in Asia and later wrote an often-criticized history of them.

hatra.name: Hatra
hatra.summary: A fortified caravan city in Upper Mesopotamia and capital of the Arab Kingdom of Hatra, flourishing in the 2nd century AD between Rome and Parthia before its destruction.

trajan.name: Trajan
trajan.summary: Roman emperor from 98 to 117 CE, one of the Five Good Emperors, whose conquests brought the empire to its greatest territorial extent; born in what is now southern Spain.

septimius-severus.name: Septimius Severus
septimius-severus.summary: Septimius Severus: Roman emperor from 193 to 211, born in Leptis Magna in the Roman province of Africa, who defeated rival claimants, sacked the Parthian capital Ctesiphon, and expanded Rome's eastern and African frontiers.

ardashir-i.name: Ardashir I
ardashir-i.summary: Founder of the Sasanian Empire (180–242 AD), who overthrew the Parthian Arsacid dynasty in 224 and took the title King of Kings, beginning ancient Iran's last pre-Islamic empire.

shapur-i.name: Shapur I
shapur-i.summary: Second Sasanian King of Kings of Iran, ruling from 240 to 270 CE, who expanded the empire and defeated two Roman emperors, capturing Valerian in 260.

parthian-empire.name: Parthian Empire
parthian-empire.summary: A major Iranian empire ruled by the Arsacid dynasty, lasting from 247 BC to 224 AD and stretching from the Euphrates to Afghanistan.

battle-of-opis.name: Battle of Opis
battle-of-opis.summary: The final 539 BC battle between the Achaemenid and Neo-Babylonian Empires, fought near the city of Opis in modern Iraq, resulting in a decisive Persian victory that ended Babylonian independence.

achaemenid-empire.name: Achaemenid Empire
achaemenid-empire.summary: Ancient Iranian empire founded by Cyrus the Great in 550 BC, the largest of its time, stretching from the Balkans to the Indus Valley before Alexander the Great conquered it in 330 BC.

sippar.name: Sippar
sippar.summary: An ancient Sumerian and later Babylonian city on the Euphrates in Iraq, where the Babylonian Map of the World was found.

cyrus-the-great.name: Cyrus the Great
cyrus-the-great.summary: Founder of the Achaemenid Empire (c. 600–530 BC), who conquered the Median, Lydian and Neo-Babylonian empires to create the largest empire of its time, known for tolerating local customs and religions.

necho-ii.name: Necho II
necho-ii.summary: A pharaoh of Egypt's 26th Dynasty (610–595 BC) whose fleet reportedly sailed around Africa, and who killed King Josiah of Judah before losing a war with Babylon.

carchemish.name: Carchemish
carchemish.summary: An ancient capital in northern Syria, ruled at times by the Mitanni, Hittite and Neo-Assyrian empires, and site of a major battle around 605 BCE mentioned in the Bible.

battle-of-carrhae.name: Battle of Carrhae
battle-of-carrhae.summary: A 53 BC battle in which Parthian cavalry lured and destroyed a Roman army led by Marcus Crassus, killing him and most of his troops in one of Rome's worst defeats.

liberators-civil-war.name: Liberators' civil war
liberators-civil-war.summary: A Roman civil war (43–42 BC) in which Mark Antony and Octavian defeated Julius Caesar's assassins, Brutus and Cassius, at the Battle of Philippi.

marcus-junius-brutus.name: Marcus Junius Brutus
marcus-junius-brutus.summary: Roman politician and orator (c.85-42 BC) best known as the leading assassin of Julius Caesar on the Ides of March, 44 BC.

gaius-cassius-longinus.name: Cassius
gaius-cassius-longinus.summary: Roman senator and general (c. 86–42 BC), a leading instigator of the plot to assassinate Julius Caesar, later defeated with Brutus at Philippi.

susa.name: Susa
susa.summary: Ancient city in what is now Iran that served as capital of Elam and winter capital of the Achaemenid Empire, remaining strategically important through the Parthian and Sasanian periods.

osroes-i.name: Osroes I
osroes-i.summary: Parthian ruler who controlled the western Parthian Empire from 109 to 129, briefly deposed in 116 when the Roman emperor Trajan installed his own puppet king.

parthamaspates-of-parthia.name: Parthamaspates
parthamaspates-of-parthia.summary: A Parthian prince installed by Rome as a client king in Mesopotamia, and later of Osroene, in the early 2nd century AD.

tel-megiddo.name: Megiddo
tel-megiddo.summary: An ancient Canaanite city-state and later royal city of Israel in northern Israel, continuously settled from about 3000 BCE and strategically placed on major trade routes.

josiah.name: Josiah
josiah.summary: 16th king of Judah, reigning around 640–609 BC, remembered for major religious reforms centralizing worship in Jerusalem and purging foreign gods.

jehoiakim.name: Jehoiakim
jehoiakim.summary: The eighteenth king of Judah, ruling from 609 to 598 BC as the second son of King Josiah; born Eliakim, he was later renamed Jehoiakim.

vologases-iv.name: Vologases IV
vologases-iv.summary: Parthian King of Kings from 147 to 191 who fought Rome from 161 to 166, briefly conquering Armenia and Syria before being pushed back and losing northern Mesopotamia.

marcus-statius-priscus.name: Marcus Statius Priscus
marcus-statius-priscus.summary: Roman senator and general active under Hadrian, Antoninus Pius and Marcus Aurelius, who served as consul in 159 CE.

ctesiphon.name: Ctesiphon
ctesiphon.summary: An ancient city on the Tigris near modern Baghdad that served as capital of the Parthian and Sasanian Persian empires for over 800 years, until falling in the 637 Muslim conquest.

pescennius-niger.name: Pescennius Niger
pescennius-niger.summary: A Roman usurper who claimed the imperial throne in 193 to 194 CE during the Year of the Five Emperors, defeated and killed by rival claimant Septimius Severus.

nusaybin.name: Nisibis
nusaybin.summary: An ancient city in northern Mesopotamia held in turn by Assyrians, Persians, Seleucids, Romans and Sasanians, and made capital of Roman Mesopotamia after a treaty in 298 CE.

diocletian.name: Diocletian
diocletian.summary: Roman emperor from 284 to 305 who ended the Crisis of the Third Century and began splitting the empire by creating the Tetrarchy, sharing rule with three co-emperors.

julian-s-persian-expedition.name: Julian's Persian Expedition
julian-s-persian-expedition.summary: A Roman campaign from March to July 363 CE in which Emperor Julian invaded Sasanian Persia, won a battle near the capital Ctesiphon, then died retreating after supply problems forced a withdrawal.

dux.name: Dux
dux.summary: Latin word for 'leader', used in the Roman Republic and early Empire for any troop commander before becoming a formal title and later the root of 'duke'.

cyrus-cylinder.name: Cyrus Cylinder
cyrus-cylinder.summary: Ancient clay cylinder inscribed in Akkadian in the name of Cyrus the Great, made after the Persian conquest of Babylon in 539 BC and discovered there in 1879; now in the British Museum.

mark-antony.name: Mark Antony
mark-antony.summary: Roman politician and general (83–30 BC) and ally of Julius Caesar who, after Caesar's assassination, formed the Second Triumvirate with Octavian and Lepidus and later allied with Cleopatra.

publius-ventidius.name: Publius Ventidius
publius-ventidius.summary: A Roman general and protégé of Julius Caesar whose victories over the Parthians avenged Crassus's earlier defeat and earned him the only triumph a Roman commander had received for beating the Parthians.

quintus-labienus.name: Quintus Labienus
quintus-labienus.summary: A Roman general (died 39 BC), son of Titus Labienus, who allied with Parthia and invaded provinces held by Mark Antony, occupying Syria and pushing into Anatolia before being defeated by Publius Ventidius.

pacorus-i.name: Pacorus I
pacorus-i.summary: Parthian prince and son of Orodes II, who led invasions into Roman-held Western Asia before being killed in battle in 38 BC.

harran.name: Harran
harran.summary: Ancient city in Upper Mesopotamia, founded between the 25th and 20th centuries BC, a major religious centre devoted to the moon god Sin and site of the 53 BC Battle of Carrhae.

ashur-uballit-ii.name: Ashur-uballit II
ashur-uballit-ii.summary: The final ruler of Assyria, from 612 to 609 BC, who rallied remaining forces after the fall of Nineveh before his defeat at Harran.

nimrod.name: Nimrod
nimrod.summary: Biblical figure in Genesis described as a mighty hunter and king in Shinar, later traditions linking him to the Tower of Babel, though no historical record of him has been found.

lilith.name: Lilith
lilith.summary: A feminine figure in Mesopotamian and Jewish mythology, first mentioned in the Dead Sea Scrolls, later described in Jewish folklore as fleeing Eden rather than submit to Adam.

book-of-esther.name: Book of Esther
book-of-esther.summary: A book of the Hebrew Bible telling how a Jewish woman becomes queen of Persia and foils a plot to kill her people, commemorated by the festival of Purim.

syriac-language.name: Syriac language
syriac-language.summary: An Eastern Aramaic dialect that emerged around the 1st century AD and became the main literary and liturgical language of Syriac Christian communities.

syriac-alphabet.name: Syriac alphabet
syriac-alphabet.summary: A right-to-left writing system used for the Syriac language since the 1st century, descended from the Aramaic alphabet and related to Hebrew and Arabic scripts.

syriac-christianity.name: Syriac Christianity
syriac-christianity.summary: A branch of Eastern Christianity expressed in the Classical Syriac language, one of Early Christianity's three major literary languages alongside Greek and Latin.

en-ma-eli.name: Enūma Eliš
en-ma-eli.summary: Babylonian creation myth from the late 2nd millennium BC, the only complete surviving account of ancient Near Eastern cosmology, recovered from the Library of Ashurbanipal.

josephus.name: Josephus
josephus.summary: Roman-Jewish historian and military leader (c. 36–100 CE) who fought Rome in the First Jewish-Roman War before surrendering, later writing The Jewish War as a key account of the revolt.

eusebius.name: Eusebius of Caesarea
eusebius.summary: Historian and bishop of Caesarea from about 314, known as the 'Father of Church history' for works including the Ecclesiastical History and a life of Emperor Constantine.

jerome.name: Jerome
jerome.summary: An early Christian priest, theologian and translator (c. 342–420) best known for translating the Bible into Latin (the Vulgate); honored as one of the four Great Latin Church Fathers.

george-syncellus.name: George Syncellus
george-syncellus.summary: Byzantine monk and chronicler who died after 810; his chronicle of world history is a key surviving source quoting the otherwise lost history of Berossus.

herodotus.name: Herodotus
herodotus.summary: Greek historian and geographer (c. 484–c. 425 BC), called 'the Father of History' for his Histories, a detailed account of the Greco-Persian Wars and the peoples and lands around them.

ctesias.name: Ctesias
ctesias.summary: A Greek physician and historian of the 5th century BC from Cnidus, then part of the Achaemenid Persian Empire.

semiramis.name: Semiramis
semiramis.summary: Semiramis: A legendary Assyrian queen, partly based on the real ninth-century BC ruler Shammuramat, credited in Greek and other traditions with a career of conquest across the Middle East and the Levant.

sardanapalus.name: Sardanapalus
sardanapalus.summary: A legendary last king of Assyria described by the Greek writer Ctesias as living in decadence and dying in self-destruction, likely a garbled memory of the real ruler Ashurbanipal.

ninus.name: Ninus
ninus.summary: According to later Greek historians, the legendary founder of Nineveh and ancient capital of Assyria, though his historical basis is uncertain.

diodorus-siculus.name: Diodorus Siculus
diodorus-siculus.summary: Ancient Greek historian from Sicily (1st century BC) who wrote the 40-book universal history Bibliotheca historica, covering world history up to about 60 BC.

quintus-curtius-rufus.name: Quintus Curtius Rufus
quintus-curtius-rufus.summary: A Roman historian, likely active in the 1st century AD, known only for his surviving work on the history of Alexander the Great; little else about his life is confirmed.

book-of-job.name: Book of Job
book-of-job.summary: A poetic book of the Hebrew Bible, likely composed during the Persian period, exploring the problem of evil through the trials of a pious man tested by suffering.

job-biblical-figure.name: Job
job-biblical-figure.summary: Central figure of the biblical Book of Job, a devout family man tested by disasters that strip away his possessions and family.

samuel-noah-kramer.name: Samuel Noah Kramer
samuel-noah-kramer.summary: An Assyriologist (1897–1990) and leading expert on Sumerian history and language, whose book History Begins at Sumer made the subject accessible to the public.

debate-between-winter-and-summer.name: Debate between Winter and Summer
debate-between-winter-and-summer.summary: A Sumerian creation myth and disputation, written on clay tablets in the mid-to-late 3rd millennium BCE, contrasting the seasons of winter and summer.

xenophon.name: Xenophon
xenophon.summary: Xenophon: Athenian-born Greek general, philosopher and historian (c. 430-355/354 BC) who was elected one of the leaders of the retreating Ten Thousand mercenaries and is remembered as one of antiquity's greatest writers.

anabasis-xenophon.name: Anabasis
anabasis-xenophon.summary: Xenophon's account, written around 370 BC, of the Ten Thousand Greek mercenaries hired by Cyrus the Younger to help him seize the Persian throne from Artaxerxes II in 401 BC.

courtyard-house.name: Courtyard house
courtyard-house.summary: A house built around a central courtyard onto which the main rooms open, sometimes with windowless or fortified exterior walls; a popular design for large English houses in the 16th century.

ziggurat-of-ur.name: Ziggurat of Ur
ziggurat-of-ur.summary: A Neo-Sumerian temple tower built in the 21st century BC by King Ur-Nammu at Ur, later restored, excavated in the 1920s–30s, and partly rebuilt under Saddam Hussein.

chogha-zanbil.name: Chogha Zanbil
chogha-zanbil.summary: An ancient Elamite ziggurat complex in Iran, built in the 14th or 13th century BCE and considered the best-preserved stepped pyramid monument, added to the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1979.

khuzestan-province.name: Khuzestan province
khuzestan-province.summary: A province in southwestern Iran bordering Iraq and the Persian Gulf, corresponding to ancient Elam whose capital was Susa; it holds Iran's largest oil field.

ur.name: Ur
ur.summary: A major Sumerian city-state in ancient Mesopotamia dating from about 3800 BC, whose patron deity was the moon god Nanna and whose ziggurat still stands partially restored.

nabopolassar.name: Nabopolassar
nabopolassar.summary: Founder of the Neo-Babylonian Empire, ruling from 626 to 605 BC; his revolt against Assyria led to that empire's destruction.

chaldean-dynasty.name: Chaldean dynasty
chaldean-dynasty.summary: The ruling dynasty of the Neo-Babylonian Empire, reigning as kings of Babylon from Nabopolassar's rise in 626 BCE until its line ended in 556 BCE.

adad-nirari-ii.name: Adad-nirari II
adad-nirari-ii.summary: King of Assyria who reigned 911–891 BCE, the first ruler of the Neo-Assyrian Empire and instigator of its major territorial expansion.

tiglath-pileser-iii.name: Tiglath-Pileser III
tiglath-pileser-iii.summary: Neo-Assyrian king (745–727 BC) who doubled Assyrian territory through brutal military reforms, marking Assyria's shift into a true empire.

ammon.name: Ammon
ammon.summary: An ancient Semitic-speaking kingdom east of the Jordan River, whose people were called Ammonites and whose chief city, Rabbah, is now Amman, Jordan's capital.

edom.name: Edom
edom.summary: An ancient kingdom south of present-day Israel, Jordan and Palestine that flourished between the 13th and 8th centuries BCE before being destroyed by the Babylonians in the 6th century BCE.

moab.name: Moab
moab.summary: An ancient kingdom in what is now southern Jordan, along the Dead Sea, known from the Mesha Stele and often in conflict with its Israelite neighbors.

kingdom-of-judah.name: Kingdom of Judah
kingdom-of-judah.summary: An ancient Israelite kingdom centered on Jerusalem, ruled for four centuries by the House of David, which became an Assyrian vassal after Tiglath-Pileser's 8th-century BC campaigns.

fall-of-nineveh.name: Battle of Nineveh
fall-of-nineveh.summary: The 612 BC siege by allied Medes and Babylonians that captured Nineveh, ending the Neo-Assyrian Empire and clearing the way for the rise of the Neo-Babylonian Empire.

nabonidus.name: Nabonidus
nabonidus.summary: Last king of the Neo-Babylonian Empire, ruling from 556 to 539 BC when Babylon fell to Cyrus the Great; regarded as an unorthodox religious reformer.

tayma.name: Tayma
tayma.summary: A Saudi Arabian city and major oasis in Tabuk Province, on the trade route between Medina and Dumah, with a long history of habitation.

belshazzar.name: Belshazzar
belshazzar.summary: Son and crown prince of Nabonidus, the last king of the Neo-Babylonian Empire, who served as regent in Babylon during his father's decade-long absence.

nebuchadnezzar-iii.name: Nebuchadnezzar III
nebuchadnezzar-iii.summary: A Babylonian noble who took the name Nebuchadnezzar and rebelled against Persian rule in 522 BC, briefly restoring Babylonian independence before his defeat.

nebuchadnezzar-iv.name: Nebuchadnezzar IV
nebuchadnezzar-iv.summary: An Urartian nobleman who seized Babylon's throne in 521 BCE, rebelling against Achaemenid Persian rule under the name of an earlier king; captured and executed the same year.

babylonian-revolts-484-bc.name: Bel-shimanni and Shamash-eriba
babylonian-revolts-484-bc.summary: Two Babylonians who separately proclaimed themselves king of Babylon and led revolts against Persian ruler Xerxes I in 484 BC, amid growing resentment of Achaemenid rule.

nidin-bel.name: Nidin-Bel
nidin-bel.summary: Possible rebel king of Babylon who briefly tried to restore native rule against the Persian Achaemenid Empire around 336 BC, known only from a fragmentary king list.

jeconiah.name: Jeconiah
jeconiah.summary: The nineteenth and penultimate king of Judah, dethroned by Babylon's Nebuchadnezzar II in the 6th century BCE and taken into captivity; Babylonian ration tablets confirm his existence in exile.

ezekiel.name: Ezekiel
ezekiel.summary: An Israelite priest and prophet who foretold Jerusalem's destruction by the Neo-Babylonian Empire in 587 BC and its later restoration; the Book of Ezekiel bears his name.

zedekiah.name: Zedekiah
zedekiah.summary: The twentieth and final king of Judah, installed by Nebuchadnezzar II after deposing his predecessor; his reign ended with Jerusalem's fall to Babylon around 586 BC.

exilarch.name: Exilarch
exilarch.summary: The hereditary leader of the Jewish community in Mesopotamia under the Parthian and Sasanian Empires and the Abbasid Caliphate, regarded as a royal heir descended from King David.

labashi-marduk.name: Labashi-Marduk
labashi-marduk.summary: Labashi-Marduk: The fifth and second-to-last king of the Neo-Babylonian Empire, ruling briefly in 556 BC before being deposed and killed in a coup led by Belshazzar.

valerian-emperor.name: Valerian
valerian-emperor.summary: Roman emperor from 253 to 260 CE, known as the first Roman emperor captured in battle, taken by the Persian emperor Shapur I after the Battle of Edessa.

edessa.name: Edessa
edessa.summary: An ancient city in Upper Mesopotamia (modern Şanlıurfa, Turkey) founded by Seleucus I Nicator, later capital of the Kingdom of Osroene and, during the Crusades, of the County of Edessa.

odaenathus.name: Odaenathus
odaenathus.summary: Founding king of the Palmyrene Kingdom, ruling from Palmyra, Syria, who defended Roman territory against the Persians after Emperor Valerian's capture in 260 and was honored with high titles by Rome.

palmyra.name: Palmyra
palmyra.summary: An ancient city in central Syria that grew wealthy from Silk Road trade caravans, reaching its height in the 260s CE under King Odaenathus and later Queen Zenobia, who rebelled against Rome.

yahwism.name: Yahwism
yahwism.summary: The ancient religion of the Israelites of Israel and Judah, centered on the god Yahweh and closely related to Canaanite religion.

yahweh.name: Yahweh
yahweh.summary: An ancient Semitic deity who became the national god of the Iron Age kingdoms of Israel and Judah, later worshipped as the sole god of Judaism.

el-deity.name: El
el-deity.summary: A Northwest Semitic word for 'god', and the name of the supreme deity of ancient Canaanite religion, described as father of the gods and creator of humanity.

canaanite-religion.name: Canaanite religion
canaanite-religion.summary: The polytheistic belief system of the ancient Levant, headed by the god El and his consort Asherah, known mainly from Ugaritic texts and archaeology.

babylonian-captivity.name: Babylonian captivity
babylonian-captivity.summary: The exile of Judeans from the Kingdom of Judah to Babylonia by the Neo-Babylonian Empire after sieges of Jerusalem in 597 and 587 BCE, ending when Persia allowed their return in 539 BCE.

second-temple-judaism.name: Second Temple Judaism
second-temple-judaism.summary: The form of Jewish religion that developed from the building of the Second Temple around 516 BCE until Jerusalem's destruction in 70 CE, marked by new religious currents and the rise of Christianity.

hellenistic-judaism.name: Hellenistic Judaism
hellenistic-judaism.summary: A form of Judaism in classical antiquity blending Jewish tradition with Hellenistic culture, centered in Alexandria and Antioch and producing the Greek Septuagint translation of the Hebrew Bible.

book-of-deuteronomy.name: Book of Deuteronomy
book-of-deuteronomy.summary: The fifth book of the Torah, presenting sermons by Moses to the Israelites before entering the Promised Land, including the Shema Yisrael, later quoted by Jesus as the Great Commandment.

sin-mythology.name: Sin (Nanna)
sin-mythology.summary: Mesopotamian god of the moon, also called Nanna, associated with cattle herding, the crescent symbol, and sometimes seen as a judge of the dead.

sheol.name: Sheol
sheol.summary: The underworld of the Hebrew Bible, a shadowy, silent realm to which the dead of all moral standing were said to go.

ereshkigal.name: Ereshkigal
ereshkigal.summary: Goddess of the land of the dead in Sumerian mythology, later said to rule the underworld Irkalla with her husband Nergal; central to the myth of Inanna's Descent into the Underworld.

ancient-mesopotamian-underworld.name: Irkalla
ancient-mesopotamian-underworld.summary: One of the Sumerian and Akkadian names for the underworld, a dark cavern beneath the earth ruled by the goddess Ereshkigal, where the dead lived on as shadows of their earthly selves.

mani-prophet.name: Mani
mani-prophet.summary: An Iranian prophet (c. 216–274 CE) who founded Manichaeism, born near Ctesiphon in the Parthian Empire and later imprisoned and killed under the Sasanian ruler Bahram I.

manichaeism.name: Manichaeism
manichaeism.summary: A major dualistic religion founded in the 3rd century CE by the prophet Mani, teaching a cosmic struggle between light and darkness and drawing on Zoroastrian, Christian and Buddhist traditions.

anu.name: Anu
anu.summary: The divine personification of the sky and king of the gods in ancient Mesopotamian religion, regarded as a source of kingship though largely passive and rarely worshipped until later centuries.

enlil.name: Enlil
enlil.summary: Ancient Mesopotamian god of wind, air, earth and storms, chief deity of the Sumerian pantheon, worshipped at the Ekur temple in Nippur from the 24th century BC.

enki.name: Ea
enki.summary: Mesopotamian god of wisdom, crafts, fresh waters and magic, first worshipped in Sumer's city of Eridu, later merged with the Semitic god Ea across Babylonia.

shamash.name: Shamash
shamash.summary: The ancient Mesopotamian sun god, believed to see everything and act as a divine judge responsible for justice, especially venerated in the cities of Sippar and Larsa.

ashur-god.name: Ashur (god)
ashur-god.summary: The national god of the Assyrians in ancient times, worshipped until their gradual conversion to Christianity between the 1st and 5th centuries AD.

church-of-the-east.name: Church of the East
church-of-the-east.summary: An Eastern Christian branch, also called the Nestorian Church, that arose from 5th-century Christological disputes and originated in Mesopotamia under the Parthian Empire.

solomon-s-temple.name: Solomon's Temple
solomon-s-temple.summary: The First Temple in Jerusalem, said in the Hebrew Bible to have been built by King Solomon and to have stood from the 10th to 6th centuries BCE before its destruction by the Babylonians.

second-temple.name: Second Temple
second-temple.summary: The temple in Jerusalem that replaced Solomon's Temple after its destruction in 587 BCE; built around 516 BCE and later expanded by Herod the Great around 18 BCE.

darius-the-great.name: Darius the Great
darius-the-great.summary: Third King of Kings of the Achaemenid Empire (522–486 BCE), who ruled it at its territorial peak, reorganized it into provinces, and commissioned the Behistun inscription.

darius-iii.name: Darius III
darius-iii.summary: Last Achaemenid King of Persia (336–330 BC), defeated by Alexander the Great in several battles before being killed by his own relative Bessus.
